content: AIDS-related diarrhoea is a significant cause of illness and death among individuals living with HIV, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where 70% of HIV-related deaths occur. This condition often severely impacts the quality of life for both individuals receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) and those who are ART-naive. In approximately 50% of cases, diarrhoea is either non-pathogenic, idiopathic, or a side effect of antiretroviral therapy, necessitating empirical antidiarrhoeal treatment. Antimotility agents, such as loperamide, diphenoxylate, and codeine, as well as adsorbents like bismuth subsalicylate, kaolin/pectin, and attapulgite, are widely available and frequently used to manage diarrhoea in these patients. Antimotility agents, which are opioid-based, work by reducing bowel activity, thereby decreasing stool output, prolonging fecal transit time, and promoting the retention of fluids and electrolytes. Adsorbents, on the other hand, function by binding to fluids, toxins, and other substances in the gut, improving stool consistency and aiding in the elimination of toxins. Given the potential role of these agents in managing chronic diarrhoea in individuals with HIV/AIDS, a review was conducted to evaluate their effectiveness in this context. The objective of the review was to assess the efficacy of antimotility agents in controlling chronic diarrhoea in people living with HIV/AIDS. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was performed in November 2006 across multiple databases, including Medline, EMBASE, the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, the Cochrane HIV/AIDS Register, and AIDSearch. Additional information was sought from the World Health Organization (WHO), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), pharmaceutical companies, and field experts. Reference lists from retrieved studies were also reviewed, regardless of language or publication status. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized controlled trials comparing an antimotility agent or an adsorbent with another antimotility agent, placebo, an adsorbent, or no treatment. The study population included children and adults diagnosed with HIV who had experienced diarrhoea for three or more weeks. Two independent reviewers selected studies and examined full-text articles for eligibility. The review identified only one trial that evaluated the use of an adsorbent, attapulgite, compared to a placebo for chronic diarrhoea in individuals with HIV/AIDS. This trial included 91 adults aged 18 to 60 years who were diagnosed with AIDS and had experienced diarrhoea for at least seven days. The results showed no evidence that attapulgite was superior to placebo in reducing stool frequency or normalizing stool consistency on days 1, 3, and 5 of treatment. The reported odds ratios were 0.34 (95% CI 0.01–8.15) on day 1, 1.35 (95% CI 0.51–3.62) on day 3, and 1.74 (95% CI 0.89–3.38) on day 5. However, this was a small trial, and its limited sample size may have reduced its ability to detect significant effects. Five deaths were reported during the study, but these were not classified according to the treatment arms. No studies assessing the use of antimotility agents were identified in the review. The authors concluded that there is currently no evidence to support the use of antimotility agents or adsorbents in controlling diarrhoea in individuals with HIV/AIDS. While the single retrieved study indicated that attapulgite was not more effective than placebo, the lack of trials evaluating antimotility agents highlights a significant gap in the evidence base. Despite this, these agents may still be used in clinical practice, with a strong emphasis on adjunctive therapies such as aggressive fluid replacement. Further research and well-designed trials are urgently needed to provide evidence-based guidance for the management of chronic diarrhoea in this population.
